en: Dīgha Nikāya 15:
Mahānidāna Sutta I.
Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How deep this dependent origination is, Bhante, and how deep it appears; yet to me it seems as clear as something plain on the palm of one’s hand.
“Do not say that, Ānanda! Do not say that, Ānanda!”
"Ānanda, this dependent origination is profound and appears profound.

It is because of the lack of realization and penetration of this Dhamma, Ānanda, that this generation has become like a tangled skein, like a knotted ball of thread, like matted rushes and reeds, and does not transcend the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realms, and saṃsāra.
‘There is aging-and-death with this as its condition,’ Ānanda—when asked thus, one should say: ‘There is.’"
“If one were to ask, ‘With what as condition is aging-and-death? one should answer, ‘With birth as condition is aging-and-death.
Being asked, ‘Does this specific condition for birth exist? you should, Ānanda, answer, ‘It does exist.
If one were to ask, ‘With what as condition is birth? one should answer, ‘With becoming as condition is birth.’”
“‘There is existence with this as its condition’—when asked thus, Ānanda, one should say, ‘There is.
If it should be asked, ‘With what as condition is there existence? one should say, ‘With clinging as condition there is existence.
‘There is clinging with this as its condition’—when asked thus, Ānanda, one should say, ‘There is.’”
“If it should be asked, ‘With what as condition does clinging arise? one should answer: ‘Clinging arises with craving as its condition.
Being asked, Ānanda, ‘Does this specific condition for craving exist? one should answer: ‘It exists.
If it should be asked, ‘With what as condition does craving arise? one should answer: ‘Craving arises with feeling as its condition.’”
“‘Is there a specific condition for feeling?’—when asked thus, Ānanda, one should answer: ‘There is.
If he should say, ‘By what condition does feeling arise?’, one should answer him: ‘Feeling arises with contact as its condition.
‘Is there a specific condition for contact?’—when asked thus, Ānanda, one should answer: ‘There is.’”
“If it should be asked, ‘With what as condition is contact? one should answer: ‘With name-and-form as condition is contact.
Being asked, Ānanda, ‘Does this specific condition for name-and-form exist? one should answer: ‘It exists.
If it should be asked, ‘With what as condition is name-and-form? one should answer: ‘With consciousness as condition is name-and-form.’”
“If one is asked, Ānanda, ‘Is there consciousness conditioned by this? one should say, ‘There is.
If it should be asked, ‘Conditioned by what is consciousness?’, one should say, ‘Consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form.
Thus, Ānanda, with name-and-form as condition there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition...”
Contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence;
with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be’: thus it has been said. And that, Ānanda, should be understood by this method: how it is that with birth as condition there is aging-and-death.

For if, Ānanda, birth were not in any way, anywhere, for anyone at all—for instance, among the gods in their state as gods, among the gandhabbas in their state as gandhabbas, among the yakkhas in their state as yakkhas, or among the bhūtas... [there would be no aging-and-death].”
or to the state of being a human among humans, to the state of being a quadruped among quadrupeds, to the state of being a bird among birds,
or to the state of being a reptile among reptiles— if, Ānanda,
for those various beings there were no birth corresponding to their respective states, then, with the total absence of birth and through the cessation of birth, would aging and death be discerned?”
“No, Bhante.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for aging-and-death, namely birth.
‘With existence as condition, there is birth’—this, Ānanda, should be understood by this method of exposition as to how with existence as condition there is birth.”
“Ānanda, if there were no existence at all, in every way and in any respect— for anyone or anywhere, namely,

existence in the sense-sphere, existence in the form-sphere, or existence in the formless-sphere— if existence were entirely absent, with the cessation of existence, would birth still be discerned? “No, indeed, venerable sir.”
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for birth, namely:

existence (*bhava*). It has been said: ‘With clinging as condition, there is existence. This, Ānanda, should be understood by way of this method: how it is that with clinging as condition there is existence.
For if, Ānanda, clinging were not to exist in any way, in any manner, in any respect, for anyone, anywhere—namely:”

“Whether it be clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, or clinging to a doctrine of self—if, in every way, there were no clinging, with the cessation of clinging, would existence be discerned?
“No, indeed, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for existence, namely: clinging.”
‘With craving as condition, clinging comes to be’: this, Ānanda, has been said; and it should be understood by this method how, with craving as condition, clinging comes to be.

For if, Ānanda, craving were entirely and in every way non-existent for anyone anywhere—that is to say, craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena—if, in the complete absence of craving, through the cessation of craving, would clinging still be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for clinging, namely craving.
As it has been said, ‘With feeling as condition, craving arises’; that, Ānanda, should be understood by this method of exposition as to how with feeling as condition, craving arises.”
For if, Ānanda, feeling did not exist in any way, in any manner, and for anyone at all— namely,
feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact,
feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact— then, with the total absence of feeling and the cessation of feeling, [craving would not arise].
“Would craving then be discerned?”—
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”—
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for craving, namely: feeling.”
Thus, Ānanda, conditioned by feeling there is craving; conditioned by craving there is pursuit; conditioned by pursuit there is gain;
conditioned by gain there is decision-making; conditioned by decision-making there is desire and lust; conditioned by desire and lust there is attachment;
conditioned by attachment there is possessiveness; conditioned by possessiveness there is stinginess.
Dependent on stinginess comes guarding.
On account of guarding, there arise many evil unwholesome states:

the taking up of sticks, the taking up of weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, accusations, divisive speech, and false speech. “On account of guarding, there arise the taking up of sticks, the taking up of weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, accusations, divisive speech, and false speech.”
‘Many evil, unwholesome states arise’—this has been said.

And so, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, on account of guarding [possessions], many evil, unwholesome states arise: taking up sticks, taking up weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, accusations, slander, and lying speech.
“Ānanda, if there were no protection at all, in every way, for anyone anywhere, then,

in the total absence of protection, with the cessation of protection, would those many evil, unwholesome phenomena— such as taking up sticks, taking up weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and lying— arise?”
“No, venerable sir.

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for the arising of many evil unwholesome states, namely: taking up sticks, taking up weapons, quarrels, disputes, contention, strife, slander, and falsehood; that is to say, watchfulness.”
“It was said: ‘Dependent upon stinginess, there is guarding. This, Ānanda, should be understood by this method: how it is that dependent upon stinginess, there is guarding.
For if, Ānanda, stinginess were not to exist in anyone at all, in any way, in any place, and if stinginess were entirely non-existent and ceased, would guarding still be discerned?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for guarding, namely, stinginess.
As for what was said—‘In dependence on possession, there is stinginess’—that, Ānanda, should be understood by this method as to how in dependence on possession there is stinginess.”

“Moreover, Ānanda, if there were no possession at all, in any way, of anything by anyone anywhere, then, with the total absence of possession and through the cessation of possession, would stinginess be discerned?
“No, indeed, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for stinginess, namely: possession.”
“It was said: ‘Possession depends upon attachment. This, Ānanda, should be understood by this method: how possession depends upon attachment.
For if, Ānanda, there were no attachment at all, in any way, of anything, anywhere—since attachment would be entirely absent, with the cessation of attachment—would possession be discerned?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for grasping, namely:
attachment. As for what was said—that ‘attachment depends upon desire and lust’—that, Ānanda, should be understood by this method: how attachment depends upon desire and lust.”

“Ānanda, if there were no sensual desire at all, in every way, for anyone, regarding anything—when sensual desire is entirely absent, with the cessation of sensual desire, would clinging be discerned?
“No, indeed, Bhante.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for clinging, namely, sensual desire.”

“It has been said, ‘Dependent on decision-making (vinicchaya), there is desire and lust. This, Ānanda, should be understood by this method: how it is that dependent on decision-making, there is desire and lust.

For if, Ānanda, decision-making were entirely and in every way non-existent for anyone anywhere, then, in the total absence of decision-making, with the cessation of decision-making, would desire and lust be discerned?
“No, indeed, Bhante.”
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for desire and lust, namely, discrimination (*vinicchaya*).
As for what was said—that ‘discrimination depends upon gain’—this, Ānanda, should be understood by the following method: how discrimination depends upon gain.
For if, Ānanda, there were no gain at all, in any way, of anything, anywhere, and if gain were entirely non-existent and ceased, would discrimination still be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for acquisition; that is to say, acquisition.
As it has been said: ‘In dependence on seeking, there is acquisition. This, Ānanda, should be understood by this method as to how in dependence on seeking, there is acquisition.”
“If, Ānanda, there were no seeking at all, in every way, entirely, and for anyone anywhere, then, with the total absence of seeking and the cessation of seeking, would gain be discerned?
“No, indeed, Bhante.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for gain, namely, seeking.”
‘With craving as condition, there is seeking’: this, Ānanda, has been said. And it should be understood by this method how, with craving as condition, there is seeking.

For if, Ānanda, craving were entirely and in every way non-existent for anyone anywhere—that is to say, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—if craving were completely absent, then with the cessation of craving, would seeking still be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for seeking, namely craving.
Thus, Ānanda, these two things converge in the single point of feeling through a twofold process.”
“It has been said, Ānanda: ‘With contact as condition, there is feeling. This, Ānanda, should be understood by this method of exposition: how it is that with contact as condition there is feeling.

For if, Ānanda, contact were entirely and in every way non-existent for anyone anywhere—namely, eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—if contact were altogether absent, with the cessation of contact, would feeling be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for feeling, namely, contact.
As it has been said: ‘With name-and-form as condition, contact,’ so it should be understood by this method how with name-and-form as condition there is contact.”
"Ānanda, by means of these aspects, these marks, these signs, and these indications, there is the designation of the mental body (nāmakāya).
In the absence of those aspects, those marks, those signs, and those indications, would tactile contact associated with naming (adhivacanasamphassa) be discernible in the physical body (rūpakāya)?"
“No, venerable sir.
“Ānanda, when those modes, those marks, those signs, and those indications by which the form-body is described are absent,
would resistance-contact still be discerned in the mind-body?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Ānanda, when those modes... those indications by which there is a designation of the mental body and the physical body do not exist—would designation-contact or resistance-contact be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Ānanda, when those modes by which... [as above] ...those indications by which there is a designation of name-and-form do not exist, would contact be discerned?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for contact, namely, name-and-form.

As it has been said, ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [comes to be],’ that, Ānanda, should be understood by this method: how it is that with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be.
For if consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would name-and-form coagulate there in the mother’s womb?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Ānanda, if consciousness, having descended into the mother’s womb, were to depart, would name-and-form come to be generated for this state of being?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Ānanda, if consciousness were to be cut off while one is still young—a boy or a girl—would name-and-form attain growth, increase, and expansion?
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for name-and-form; that is to say, consciousness.”
‘With name-and-form as condition, consciousness’: thus it has been said. Now, Ānanda, by this method it should be understood how with name-and-form as condition there is consciousness.
For if, Ānanda, consciousness were not to find a footing in name-and-form, would there then be the manifestation of the origination of suffering—the arising of birth, aging, and death—in the future?
“No, indeed, Bhante.”
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for consciousness, namely, name-and-form.
To this extent, Ānanda, one is born, or ages, or dies, or passes away, or reappears.
To this extent there is a range for designation, to this extent a range for language, to this extent a range for description.”

This is the domain of wisdom; to this extent the round proceeds for the purpose of describing this state of being, namely, that name-and-form together with consciousness proceed through their mutual conditionality.
2. The Description of the Self.
And in what way, Ānanda, does one describing a self describe it?
For one describing a limited material self describes it thus:
"My self is material and limited."
For indeed, Ānanda, when one describes the self as having form and infinite, one describes it thus:
‘My self has form and is infinite.
Or indeed, Ānanda, when one describes the self as formless and limited, one describes it thus: [‘My self is formless and limited’].”
‘My self is formless and limited.
Or, Ānanda, when one describes a self that is formless and infinite, one describes it thus:
‘My self is formless and infinite.’
In this regard, Ānanda, one who describes the self as having form and being limited does so either by describing the self as having form and being limited in the present,
or by describing the self as having form and being limited in the future, or else thinking, "Though it is not so now, I will bring it about that it becomes so."
Or else it occurs to him thus:
"This being so, Ānanda, it is appropriate to say that the view 'the self is material and limited' underlies his mind.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for one who describes the self as material and infinite:
Either he now describes the self as having form and infinite,
or he describes the self as having form and infinite to be realized there [in the future], or else he thinks: "Though it is not so,
I shall make it become such."
This being so, Ānanda, it is appropriate to say that the underlying tendency toward the view of a self as possessing form and being infinite persists.
In this regard, Ānanda, concerning one who describes the self as formless and limited:
either he describes the self as formless and limited in the present, or he describes it as such in the future. Or else... [he describes] the self as formless...
One who describes a limited self describes it thus: "I shall make what is not so become so," or such a thought occurs to him.
This being so, Ānanda, it is appropriate to say that the view of a limited immaterial self underlies his mind.
In this regard, Ānanda, one who describes the self as formless and infinite does so either by describing the self as formless and infinite at present,
or by describing the self as formless and infinite in the future, thinking: "Though it is not yet so, I will bring it to suchness."
Or else it occurs to him thus:
"While this is so, Ānanda, it is appropriate to say that the view of a formless self as infinite underlies his mind.
To this extent, Ānanda, one who describes a self does so.
3. The Description of Self.
And in what way, Ānanda, does one who does not describe a self not describe it?
By not describing a material self, limited, Ānanda, one does not describe it.
‘My self is material and limited.
For, Ānanda, when one does not describe the self as material and infinite, one does not describe it thus:
‘My self is material and infinite.’
For, Ānanda, when one does not describe a formless self as limited, one does not describe it thus:
‘My formless self is limited.
And, Ānanda, when one does not describe a formless self as infinite, one does not describe it thus: [‘My formless self is infinite’].”
‘My self is formless and infinite.
In this regard, Ānanda, one who does not describe the self as having form and being limited—
whether he does not describe it as such now, or [does not describe it as such] regarding what will come to be there— [does not describe it thus].”
Thus, not describing a self as material and limited, he does not describe it;
nor does he have the thought, "Though it is not such, I will make it become such.
Since this is the case, Ānanda, it is appropriate to say that the view of a self as material and limited does not underlie his mind.
In this regard, Ānanda, he who does not describe the self as finite and material neither describes it as such now,
nor does he describe it as finite and material in the future, nor does he describe it as being thus when it is actually not thus.
Or else, Ānanda, it does not occur to him: ‘I shall make [the self] subservient to me.
This being so, Ānanda, it is appropriate to say that the view of a finite self possessing form does not underlie his mind.
In this regard, Ānanda, he who does not describe the self as formless and limited does not describe it thus.
Now, he does not describe a self as formless and limited; nor does he describe it as one that will become formless and limited in the future;
nor does he think, "Though this is not so, I shall make it such."
This being so, Ānanda, it is fitting to say: "The view of a self as formless and limited does not underlie [consciousness].

In this regard, Ānanda, one who does not describe a self that is formless and infinite—whether he does not describe such a self now, or whether he does not describe a future self there—[does not describe it].
Thus, not describing a self as formless and infinite, he does not describe it;
nor does he think, “I shall bring about what is not such as being such.
Since this is so, Ānanda, it is fitting to say that the view of a self as formless and infinite does not underlie his mind.
"To this extent, Ānanda, one who does not designate a self does not designate it.
4. Contemplation of a Self:
To what extent, Ānanda, does one who contemplates a self contemplate it?"
For when one regards feeling as self, Ānanda, one regards it thus:
"Feeling is my self.
Or else, Ānanda, when regarding self, one regards it thus: "Feeling is not my self; my self is without the experience of feeling."
“‘Feeling is certainly not my self, nor is my self devoid of feeling; rather, my self feels, for my self has the nature of feeling’—in this way, Ānanda, one who regards the self regards it.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for the one who says:
‘Feeling is my self’...”
He should be addressed thus:
"Friend, there are these three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
“Of these three feelings, which one do you regard as the self?
“Ānanda, at the time when one feels a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a painful feeling, nor does one feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
at that time, one feels only a pleasant feeling.”
Ānanda, at whatever time one experiences a painful feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
at that time, one experiences only a painful feeling.
Ānanda, at whatever time one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling, nor does one experience a painful feeling.
At that time, one experiences only neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
But, Ānanda, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Painful feeling too, Ānanda, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, even the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
When one experiences a pleasant feeling, the thought occurs: ‘This is my self.
But with the cessation of that very pleasant feeling, the thought occurs: ‘My self has vanished.’”
When experiencing a painful feeling, one thinks, "This is my self.
Upon the cessation of that very painful feeling, one thinks, "My self has departed.
When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one thinks, "This is my self."
With the cessation of that very feeling which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the thought occurs: ‘My self has departed.
Thus, even in this present life, he who says, ‘Feeling is my self,’ regards the self as impermanent, mixed with pleasure and pain, and subject to arising and passing away.
Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not acceptable to regard feeling as one’s self.
In this regard, Ānanda, whoever says:
"Feeling is certainly not my self; my self is devoid of feeling," should be asked:
"But friend, where there is absolutely no feeling, could the thought 'I am this' possibly occur there?"
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not acceptable to regard [the self] thus: ‘Feeling is certainly not my self; my self is devoid of feeling.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for one who speaks thus:”
‘Feeling is certainly not my self, nor is my self devoid of feeling; rather, it is my self that feels, for my self is subject to feeling.
To him, one should say:
“Friend, suppose that feelings were to cease entirely, in every way, and without remainder.”
“If, entirely, feeling were not to exist, and with the cessation of feeling, would there then be the thought, ‘I am this’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Ānanda, by this it is not acceptable to regard it thus: ‘Feeling is certainly not my self; nor is my self devoid of feeling; my self feels, for my self has the nature of feeling.’”
But when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not regard feeling as self, nor does he regard what is devoid of feeling as self, nor does he regard it thus: "Self feels;
for my self has the nature of feeling," then, not regarding things in this way, he does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains nibbāna.
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Ānanda, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, it would be improper for anyone to say of him:
‘The Tathāgata exists after death; such is his view.’”
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’—this is his view; that is improper.
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’—this is his view; that is improper.
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—this is his view; that is improper.
For what reason?
To whatever extent there is designation, Ānanda, to whatever extent there is the range of designation; to whatever extent there is language, to whatever extent there is the range of language;

to whatever extent there is description, to whatever extent there is the range of description; to whatever extent there is wisdom, to whatever extent there is the domain of wisdom; to whatever extent there is the round [of saṃsāra]—

Insofar as it is appropriate: for a bhikkhu liberated through direct knowledge, it would be improper to hold the view, "He does not know and does not see that bhikkhu liberated through direct knowledge.
5. The Seven Stations of Consciousness.
"There are, Ānanda, seven stations of consciousness and two bases.
Which seven?
There are beings, Ānanda, who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation."
This is the first station of consciousness.
There are, Ānanda, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who have first reappeared there.
This is the second station of consciousness.
There are, Ānanda, beings who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara devas.
This is the third station of consciousness.
There are, Ānanda, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas.
This is the fourth station of consciousness.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," have reached the sphere of infinite space.
This is the fifth station of consciousness.
Ānanda, there are beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," have reached the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the sixth station of consciousness.
Ānanda, there are beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," have reached the base of nothingness.
This is the seventh station of consciousness.
The sphere of non-percipient beings and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are the second [station].

In this regard, Ānanda, as for this first station of consciousness—those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as human beings, certain devas, and certain beings in the states of deprivation—this is it.
"Ānanda, if one understands that [sensation], understands its origin, understands its passing away,
understands its gratification, understands its danger, and understands the escape from it, would it be appropriate for such a person to delight in it?"
“No, venerable sir.
… [as before] … “In this regard, Ānanda, there is this sphere of non-percipient beings.
Now, Ānanda, whoever understands that, understands its origin and its passing away.”
“He understands it, he understands its gratification, he understands its danger, and he understands the escape from it—
is it fitting for him to delight in that?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“In this regard, Ānanda, as for this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
whoever, Ānanda, understands that, understands its origin, understands its passing away,
understands its gratification, understands its danger, and understands the escape from it— ”
“Does he understand this? Would it be appropriate for him to delight in that?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“But when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands these seven stations of consciousness and these two spheres...”
Having understood, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these things, one is liberated through non-clinging;
Ānanda, such a bhikkhu is called "liberated by wisdom.
6. The Eight Liberations.
"Ānanda, there are these eight liberations.
Which eight?
Possessing form, one sees forms."
This is the first liberation.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally;
this is the second liberation.
He is intent only upon the beautiful;
this is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This is the fourth liberation.
Having completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceiving "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness;
this is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness;
this is the sixth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the seventh liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling;
this is the eighth liberation.
"These, Ānanda, are the eight liberations.
When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu enters upon these eight liberations in forward order, in reverse order, and in both forward and reverse order;
when he enters them wherever he wishes, in whatever way he wishes, and for as long as he wishes—"
"He enters into them and emerges from them.
And with the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he dwells having attained it.
This, Ānanda, is called a bhikkhu who is liberated both ways. And, Ānanda, there is no other liberation both ways higher or more sublime than this."
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahānidāna Sutta, the second, is finished.
